title: Seller-Paid Rate Buydowns: A Tool Every Agent Should Know
description: Seller-paid buydowns can lower a buyer's payment and help listings sell. Here's how temporary and permanent buydowns work and how agents can use them well.
image_alt: A couple signing documents together at a desk

faq.a: A temporary buydown reduces the borrower's effective interest rate for the first year or years of the loan. The cost is paid up front, often by the seller, and held in an account that subsidizes the payments.

faq.q: Does the buyer qualify at the lower rate?
faq.a: Generally no. Under Fannie Mae guidelines, for example, the borrower must qualify at the full note rate, not the reduced rate.

faq.q: Is a buydown better than a price reduction?
faq.a: It depends on the buyer. A buydown can lower the early payments more than an equivalent price reduction, while a price cut permanently lowers the loan amount.

body_html:
When buyers are stretched on monthly payments, a small price reduction often doesn't move the needle. A seller-paid rate buydown can. For listing agents, it's a way to make a home more affordable without cutting the headline price. For buyer's agents, it's a negotiation tool that speaks directly to what buyers care about most: the payment.

Two types of buydowns

Temporary buydownPermanent buydown
How it worksReduces the effective rate for the first year or yearsDiscount points lower the rate for the life of the loan
FundsHeld in an account that subsidizes early paymentsPaid at closing
Best forBuyers expecting income growth or planning to refinanceBuyers planning to keep the loan long term

How temporary buydowns work

With a temporary buydown, the borrower's effective rate is reduced for an initial period and then steps up to the full note rate. Common structures reduce the rate for one or two years. The cost of the subsidy is paid up front, often by the seller as a concession, and deposited into an account that covers the difference each month.

Under Fannie Mae's temporary buydown guidelines, sellers, lenders, and others can fund them, the buyer must qualify at the full note rate, and they're limited to primary residences and second homes. Other programs have their own rules.

How permanent buydowns work

With a permanent buydown, the seller's credit pays for discount points that lower the interest rate for the entire loan. The monthly savings are smaller in the early years than a temporary buydown might provide, but they last as long as the buyer keeps the loan.

Buydown vs. price reduction

For the same seller cost, a buydown often lowers the buyer's early payments more than a price cut would. A price cut, on the other hand, permanently reduces the loan amount and makes the appraisal easier to support. The right answer depends on the buyer's goals:

  • Payment relief now: a temporary buydown
  • Lower cost over the long term: a permanent buydown or price reduction
  • Less cash to close: a closing cost credit, covered in my post on seller credits

Rules agents need to know

  1. Concession limits apply. Seller-funded buydowns count toward the program's limits on interested party contributions.
  2. The buyer still qualifies at the full rate. A buydown improves affordability but usually doesn't increase purchasing power.
  3. Investment properties may not be eligible for temporary buydowns under some guidelines.
  4. Get the structure right in the contract. Coordinate with the loan officer on wording so the funds can be used as intended.

Using buydowns as a listing strategy

Instead of a price reduction, some listing agents advertise that the seller will contribute toward a rate buydown for a qualified buyer. This can attract buyers focused on monthly payment. Keep any advertising compliant: avoid quoting specific rates or payments unless all required disclosures are included, and partner with a lender on the details.

Buyers don't buy prices; they buy payments. A buydown speaks their language.

Talking to buyers about buydowns

Be clear with buyers that a temporary buydown is temporary. The payment will rise to the full note rate after the buydown period. Buyers should be comfortable with the full payment from day one. Some plan to refinance if rates fall, but that's never guaranteed. A good loan officer will show the payment in every year of the buydown so there are no surprises.

Coordinating the details in escrow

Buydowns are simple in concept but have moving parts. Here's what to coordinate so the funds land where they should:

  1. Confirm the structure early. Temporary or permanent, and which program, before you write it into the counteroffer.
  2. Use clear contract language. Spell out that the seller credit is to be applied toward a rate buydown, and confirm the wording with the loan officer.
  3. Check the cost. The loan officer will calculate the exact cost of the buydown based on the loan amount and structure.
  4. Watch the cap. Combined credits, including closing costs and the buydown, must fit within the program's concession limit.
  5. Review the disclosures. The buyer's Closing Disclosure should reflect the buydown funds correctly.

When everyone is aligned up front, a buydown adds little complexity to escrow. When it's added at the last minute, it can create redisclosure timing issues and delays, so build it in early.

Explaining buydowns to sellers

Sellers sometimes hesitate because a buydown sounds complicated. Keep it simple: instead of lowering the price, the seller contributes a credit that makes the buyer's early payments more affordable. For many sellers, that's an easier pill to swallow than a visible price cut, and it can attract more buyers who are focused on monthly cost. Show the seller a side-by-side of net proceeds under each option so they can decide with numbers, not assumptions.

The takeaway

Seller-paid buydowns are a powerful, often underused tool. Understand the difference between temporary and permanent buydowns, respect concession limits, and make sure buyers can afford the full payment. Bring the loan officer in early, and you'll have a smart alternative the next time a price reduction alone isn't enough.
